summary: Proposes experimental improvements for IP multicast in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain: a multicast tree mobility anchor as the anchor point for multicast traffic, and a direct routing option where the access gateway gets content from the local network. The goals are less duplicated traffic and support for varied deployments.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone moves around, video meant for many viewers should not be copied again and again. These tricks save copies.

questions: what is a multicast tree mobility anchor
subtitle: Optimizing multicast delivery when mobile nodes move between network gateways.

tldr.problem: When mobile nodes roam between access gateways in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, multicast traffic can be unnecessarily duplicated as multiple tunnels carry the same stream to the same gateway.
tldr.mechanism: Two complementary optimizations: a Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor (MTMA) that acts as the centralized multicast source for remote content, and direct routing that lets gateways fetch local multicast content directly from nearby routers.
tldr.outcome: Experimental methods to reduce multicast duplication in mobile networks. Later work on multicast in PMIPv6 built on these ideas.

today: RFC 7028 is an Experimental protocol. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It provides optimization techniques for multicast in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains and influenced later work on multicast mobility.

sections.title: The Multicast Duplication Problem
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) allows mobile nodes to move between access gateways while maintaining continuous unicast connectivity through tunnels to the Local Mobility Anchor (LMA). However, PMIPv6 was designed for unicast traffic. When multicast is added, the same multicast stream can arrive at one gateway through multiple unicast tunnels—one for each mobile node subscribed to that group from a different LMA.

RFC 7028 proposes two optimizations: a Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor (MTMA) to aggregate multicast subscriptions at a single point, and direct routing to fetch local content efficiently without tunneling.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now the same video arrives at a gateway multiple times, once per person watching it. Instead, one copy should arrive and get sent to everyone.

sections.title: Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor (MTMA)
sections.content:
The MTMA is a centralized router that acts as the multicast source point for all remote content in a PMIPv6 domain. Mobile access gateways (MAGs) establish multicast tunnels to the MTMA and act as Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) proxies toward their attached mobile nodes. When an MN joins a multicast group, the MAG aggregates that subscription and forwards it to the MTMA via the tunnel. The MTMA then replicates the multicast stream once per tunnel, avoiding the tunnel convergence problem.

The MTMA uses existing PMIPv6 security mechanisms (tunnel establishment, heartbeat) and operates transparently to the mobile nodes, which need not be aware of MTMA.
sections.plainLanguage: One special friend (MTMA) is the entry point for all outside videos. Each cell tower tells this friend who wants which video, and the friend sends one copy per tower.

sections.title: Direct Routing for Local Content
sections.content:
Direct routing allows MAGs to bypass the MTMA and fetch multicast content directly from local multicast routers. The MAG's MLD proxy upstream interface connects to a local multicast router (or another MLD proxy) rather than the MTMA. This is beneficial when content is available locally and reduces tunneling overhead.

The choice between MTMA subscription and direct routing can be configured statically at the MAG or determined dynamically by the LMA using a new Dynamic IP Multicast Selector mobility option in Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages. This option specifies, per multicast group, whether traffic should be routed locally or to the MTMA.
sections.plainLanguage: If the video is made locally, the tower can just grab it from the local provider instead of asking the special friend across the network.

sections.title: Signaling and Multicast Subscription
sections.content:
When a mobile node attaches to a MAG, the MAG establishes a unicast PMIPv6 tunnel to the LMA and a multicast tunnel to the MTMA (or configures direct routing). The MAG then acts as an MLD proxy: it solicits multicast group memberships from the MN, aggregates reports from multiple MNs into a single upstream report, and forwards it to the MTMA or local multicast router.

During handover, the new MAG detects the mobile node, establishes new tunnels, issues MLD queries, collects subscription reports, and subscribes to the required groups. The base multicast specification (RFC 6224) handles most signaling; this RFC adds the optimization enhancements.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone says 'I want this video.' The tower tells its special friend or the local provider. When the phone moves, the new tower asks the phone again what it wants.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content: The RFC describes four deployment scenarios in Appendix A: 1:1 (one MAG per LMA), N:1 (multiple MAGs per LMA), 1:N (one MAG per LMA but many LMAs), and H-LMA (hybrid LMA serving both unicast and multicast). Each scenario has different characteristics for MTMA placement and tunnel efficiency. MTMA can be standalone or co-located with the LMA; direct routing is chosen based on local content availability and operator preference.
sections.plainLanguage: Depending on how many towers and home anchors there are, the special friend (MTMA) might be in different places or even combined with the unicast anchor.
